extracted.intended_audience: scientists, students, and practitioners of physics/metrology studying units and standards of measurement
extracted.subtask_short: defining units and standards of measurement
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing, defining, and perpetuating standard units of time, length, mass, and derived quantities; compares candidate standards (bar, terrestrial, pendulum, natural constants), recommends practical and theoretical principles, and discusses provisional/derived units and dimensional analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultimate chronometry standard should be founded on a physically constant body
rubrics_metrics.description: "The ultimate standard of chronometry must be founded on the physical properties of some body of more constant character than the earth; for instance, a carefully arranged metallic spring, hermetically sealed in an exhausted glass vessel."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes objections (changes in dimensions/elasticity of wrought metal over millions of years) and records Maxwell's novel suggestion that undulations of light in vacuo would form the most universal standard of reference, with the unit of time equal to the time of one vibration of the light whose wavelength is taken as the unit of length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pendulum is unsuitable as an absolute time standard
rubrics_metrics.description: "The pendulum, although so admirable an instrument for subdivision of time, fails as a standard; for though the same pendulum affected by the same force of gravity performs equal vibrations in equal times, yet the slightest change in the form or weight of the pendulum, the least corrosion of any part, or the most minute displacement of the point of suspension, falsifies the results..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists additional difficulties: temperature, friction, resistance, length of vibration, and practical issues of observing undulations with requisite accuracy; pendulum useful as accessory but not ultimate standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard length ideally defined by one single object
rubrics_metrics.description: "The standard length must be defined by one single object. To make two bars of exactly the same length...is beyond the power of human art."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains problem if multiple copies declared equally correct (future discrepancies lead to disputes); notes practical difficulties in defining terminal points on bars and proving substances remain invariable in dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bar (artifact) standard: practical advantages and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocates using a single preserved bar metre/yard as practical standard because successive generations can compare copies to the one standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges difficulty of constructing and preserving an invariable bar and of proving absolute invariability of any substance; nevertheless the bar standard is preferred practically and the international practice reverted to a bar metre when earth-based definition proved inaccurate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terrestrial (earth-based) standard is problematic
rubrics_metrics.description: The method assuming the globe as ultimate standard (e.g., metre = ten-millionth part of quadrant) is imperfect because the earth is not invariable in size and accurate comparison requires elaborate trigonometrical survey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives historic example: French metre found erroneous by one part in 5527 and thus the relation to the earth was abandoned in favor of a bar standard; notes earth's slow contraction and geological changes as reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pendulum-length (seconds pendulum) standard for space is inferior
rubrics_metrics.description: Defining length by the seconds pendulum (Huyghens' proposal) requires assuming gravity and sidereal day are invariable; the method makes one physical quantity depend on two others (time and force).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical difficulties: determining centre of oscillation, air resistance/buoyancy corrections, electrical attractions; Kater's reversible pendulum and Gauss' methods still face severe practical issues. Conclusion: pendulum cannot compete with bar standard in accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetuation principle: compare many materials and use agreement/mean
rubrics_metrics.description: "The best principle...is that, if a variation of length occurs, it will in all probability be of different amount in different substances. If then a great number of standard metres were constructed of all kinds of different metals and alloys...careful comparison would show...the standard would be furnished by the mean length of those which agreed most closely with each other."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposes constructing standards from diverse materials (metals, rocks, porcelain, glass) and taking the mean of the most concordant to detect and reduce material-specific variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit of density should be a uniform, reproducible substance (e.g., water at defined temperature)
rubrics_metrics.description: "For the unit of density we may assume that of any substance which is uniform in quality, and can readily be referred to from time to time. Pure water at any definite temperature, for instance that of snow melting under inappreciable pressure, furnishes an invariable standard of density."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains using gravity and balance comparisons (Newton/Gauss pendulum experiments) to determine comparative densities; compares equal bulks with equal bulk of standard water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a provisional artifact (kilogram prototype) for mass due to measurement practicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Although unit of mass ought to be cubic unit of matter of standard density, the metric founders took the cubic centimetre of water as the gram; practically, a preserved kilogram prototype (platinum/iridium) is used as provisional mass standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes difficulty of determining volume of water exactly; weights can be compared far more precisely (one part in a million), so using a durable artifact allows greatest practical exactness while leaving determination in terms of space/density for future work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural constants (light wavelengths, atomic weights) are theoretically best standards but currently impractical
rubrics_metrics.description: "The vibrations of light and the atoms of matter might conceivably be employed as the ultimate standards of length, time, and mass...the wave-length in vacuum of a particular kind of light...would be the most universal standard of length."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States these are likely the most fixed phenomena theoretically, but presently impractical because we cannot measure vibration periods or atomic masses with the accuracy attainable by artifact comparison; recommends determining wavelengths and absolute atomic weights in terms of existing standards for future reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce subsidiary/new units only if they assist precise expression and relate to primary units
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is allowable for a scientific man to introduce a new unit in any branch of knowledge, provided that it assists precise expression, and is carefully brought into relation with the primary units."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives chemical examples (Williamson's volume unit; Hofmann's 'crith') and notes these must be subordinate and ultimately defined by primary units, not introducing new assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derived units should follow naturally from base units to simplify relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Derived units (area, volume, velocity, momentum, force, energy) should be defined from primary units of space, time, and mass so relations between different quantities are simple and natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains examples: area = L^2, volume = L^3, velocity = L/T, momentum = mass*velocity, force = momentum/time, energy = force*space; adopting such derived units eases comprehension and calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use provisional units physically defined and reproducible when primary relations unknown
rubrics_metrics.description: For phenomena whose relation to primary units is not yet known (e.g., light, heat), select a provisional unit of convenient, reproducible intensity defined by physical circumstances so experiments can proceed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Bunsen and Roscoe's unit of light; unit of heat often taken as that which raises one gram of water by 1°C. Later, the relation of these provisional units to primary units (energy) can be determined when measurements improve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the theory of dimensions to understand interdependence of quantities
rubrics_metrics.description: "In order to understand the relations between the quantities dealt with in physical science, it is necessary to pay attention to the Theory of Dimensions...This theory investigates the manner in which each derived unit depends upon or involves one or more of the fundamental units."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives how to denote dimensions (length L, time T, density D, mass M) and examples: area L^2, volume L^3, velocity L T^-1; emphasizes dimensional analysis as a tool for checking and forming relations between physical quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a single, widely-agreed system of units (prefer metric) for convenience and comparability
rubrics_metrics.description: "It would evidently be a source of great convenience if scientific men could agree upon some single system of units...Statements would thus be rendered easily comparable...It seems to be generally allowed...that the metric system...presents the best basis for the ultimate system."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that metric system is simple, scientific, established in Western Europe, legalized in England, commonly used by scientists, and should be accepted at least in main features to save labor and make literature intelligible.
